about: How Lunenburg compares with the towns it borders, the towns this project uses as peers, the towns the math says resemble it, and the places its children are actually schooled: tax bills, overrides, per-pupil spending and the commercial share of the base.

conclusions.basis: dls-avg-tax-bill.csv and dls-new-growth.csv at FY2026, over the 161 single-town K–12 districts. Pearson correlation on the levels.
conclusions.claim: The tax bill tracks home value (r +0.91) and income (r +0.92). New growth: r -0.03.
conclusions.detail: Across the 161 Massachusetts towns that run their own K–12 district, the average single-family tax bill correlates with the average single-family value at r +0.91 and with DOR income per capita at r +0.92. Those two sit close enough that nothing here separates them, and they are largely measuring the same thing: towns with expensive houses have wealthy households in them. Against the new growth a town certifies onto its levy limit — the measure of what it built — the correlation is r -0.03, which is no relationship at all. The commercial share of the base does a little better at r -0.38, and still nothing like the house.

value_bill.unit: correlation between average home value and average tax bill, 161 towns

conclusions.not_shown: Which way any of it runs. A town with expensive houses can afford a higher bill and also chooses one; nothing here separates the two. And a correlation across towns in one year is not what would happen to one town’s bill if its commercial base grew — that is a different question, asked on /growth.

see.label: What commercial growth would have to look like

conclusions.so_what: What a household pays follows what its house is worth and what it earns, not what the town built.

conclusions.basis: Select Board minutes, 25 November 2025, the tax classification hearing: the Principal Assessor’s split-rate analysis as the minute records it. The average bill and average value in the same minute are compared against dls-avg-tax-bill.csv at FY2026.
conclusions.claim: Shifting the most the law allows onto commercial saves a $350,000 home $224.25 a year.
conclusions.detail: The correlation above says a commercial base does not show up as a smaller residential bill. Lunenburg’s own Principal Assessor priced exactly that, for this town, at the Select Board’s tax classification hearing on 25 November 2025. Lunenburg levies a SINGLE rate, $14.39 per thousand in FY2026. At the maximum allowable CIP shift of 1.50 the residential rate would fall to $13.70 and the commercial rate rise to $21.58 — worth $224.25 to a $350,000 home, and about $2,336.75 more on a comparable commercial property. Her figures reconcile to the state’s: the minute states an average single-family bill of $7,443.89 on an average value of $517,296, and the Division of Local Services publishes $7,444 on $517,296.

saving.unit: a year off a $350,000 home, at the largest shift onto commercial the statute permits

conclusions.not_shown: We did not recompute her split-rate arithmetic; the rates and the two property figures are as the minute states them, and rule 13a applies — a figure a person assembled is stated, however official the document. What raises confidence is the part that CAN be checked: her average bill and average value match the state’s file for the same year exactly. The minute also reports that of the 351 communities only 112 have adopted a split rate and only 7 of those have a CIP share at or below a tenth; nothing held here lists which towns split, so that count is hers and is not verified.

see.label: What commercial growth would have to look like

conclusions.so_what: The town’s assessor recommended against it. A shift moves the bill between classes, not the levy.

conclusions.basis: DESE per-pupil total expenditures at SY2025 and DLS bills at FY2026, over the 161-town frame; cohort by root-mean z-distance on the eight structural measures.
conclusions.claim: Of the towns most like Lunenburg, 9 of 10 spend more per pupil and 7 charge less.
conclusions.detail: The 10 towns are chosen by distance in a standardised space on eight things a town does not decide: how many children, how many are low income, how many are English learners, how many have disabilities, how many are placed out of district, the average house, income per capita and the commercial share of the base. Spending and bills are deliberately NOT among them, so they can be compared afterwards rather than assumed. Lunenburg’s $18,027 per pupil in SY2025 is 158th of 161; the 10 towns run from $17,188 to $26,738.

more.unit: look-alike towns spending more per pupil than Lunenburg

conclusions.not_shown: That any of them educates a child better, or worse. Per-pupil spending is all funds divided by full-time-equivalent pupils and says nothing about outcomes. Nor is it the town’s bill: it includes state aid, grants, circuit breaker and every other fund, so a town spending more per pupil is not necessarily taxing more for it.
conclusions.so_what: Lunenburg is 158th of 161 comparable districts on spending per pupil.

conclusions.basis: DESE per-pupil total expenditures and total FTE pupils, SY2011 and SY2025, multiplied per district; compound annual rate over 14 years.
conclusions.claim: On TOTAL school spending growth Lunenburg is 7th of 11: 3.2% a year.
conclusions.detail: Per-pupil spending is a ratio, and the gap above is mostly its denominator. Total spending — per-pupil times full-time-equivalent pupils, which is DESE’s own arithmetic run backwards — grew 3.2% a year at Lunenburg from SY2011 to SY2025, against 2.2% to 4.6% across the same 10 towns, putting it 7th of 11. What separates them is pupils: Lunenburg’s full-time-equivalent enrolment fell 5.1%, and 10 of the 10 look-alikes fell further, one of them by 34.4%. Across the whole frame, losing enrolment and raising per-pupil spending go together at r -0.56.

total_cagr.unit: a year growth in Lunenburg’s total school spending, SY2011–SY2025

conclusions.not_shown: Why Lunenburg held its enrolment while these towns did not. Births, housing turnover, school choice and the boundary of who counts all move that number and none of them is separated here. Total spending is also all funds, so part of the growth is state aid and grants rather than the town’s levy — the split is not published per line.
conclusions.so_what: It kept its pupils. The look-alikes lost more, which lifts per-pupil without spending more.

conclusions.basis: Both cohorts computed over the same 161-town frame; membership of the two closest-10 lists intersected, then the closest-25 lists.
conclusions.claim: 0 of 10 — no town is closest to Lunenburg on both what it is and what it does.
conclusions.detail: Two cohorts were built from the same 161 towns. One matches on structure — children, need, housing, income, commercial base. The other matches on behaviour — the tax bill, the bill as a share of income, per-pupil spending, how many override questions have been put and won, and the trend in the bill, in spending and in enrolment. The closest 10 lists share no town. Widen both to 25 and 9 towns appear on both. The nearest on structure is Swansea at a distance of 0.391; the nearest on behaviour is Auburn at 0.507.

overlap.unit: towns in both closest lists — structure and behaviour

conclusions.not_shown: That either cohort is the right one. A distance is a statement about the measures given equal weight and nothing more; a different weighting gives different towns. What the empty intersection does show is that the answer to "who is like us" depends entirely on which question is being asked.
conclusions.so_what: 9 towns make the closest 25 on both. Resembling Lunenburg and acting like it are different.

conclusions.basis: dls-override-votes.csv, wins per town, against dls-avg-tax-bill.csv at FY2026, over the 161-town frame.
conclusions.claim: Towns that have won more overrides charge higher bills: r +0.61 across 161 towns.
conclusions.detail: Every override the state records for these towns since FY1990, counted by wins, correlates with the FY2026 average single-family bill at r +0.61. Lunenburg has put 10 questions and won 4, raising $2,010,875 of permanent levy capacity. An override is not a one-year charge: it raises the levy limit for ever, and the limit compounds at 2.5% a year from wherever it is left. That is the mechanism the statute describes, and it is why a vote taken decades ago is still inside today’s bill.

won_bill.unit: correlation between overrides won and the average tax bill, 161 towns

conclusions.not_shown: Which causes which, and it matters here. A town with a higher bill may pass overrides because it can afford them, rather than having a higher bill because it passed them. The correlation is equally consistent with both, and with a third thing — wealth — driving each. Nor does a won amount mean the town levied it: an override raises the ceiling, and a town may sit below its own limit.
conclusions.so_what: Lunenburg won $2,010,875 of permanent capacity across 4 wins. A won override never expires.

conclusions.basis: dese-town-enrollment.csv, Lunenburg rows at FY2026, grouped by what kind of district each destination is.
conclusions.claim: Of 177 Lunenburg children schooled elsewhere, 32 go where one town’s taxes pay.
conclusions.detail: In FY2026, 177 Lunenburg children were enrolled somewhere other than Lunenburg’s own schools, out of 1,730 in total. 97 of them are at Montachusett Regional Vocational Technical, which Lunenburg is a member of and pays an assessment to — so that is not a departure from the tax base. 38 are at charter or Commonwealth virtual schools, which no single town funds. 10 are in regional districts split across member towns with different bills. That leaves 32 at districts one town’s taxpayers pay for, where a tax bill can honestly be set beside a per-pupil figure.

one_town.unit: of the 177 children schooled outside Lunenburg’s own schools attend one that a single town’s taxpayers fund

conclusions.not_shown: What any of it costs. A count of children is not a tuition, a charter assessment or an assessment share — rule 11 — and this says nothing about which fund pays. It also cannot say why a family chose a destination; the file records where a child is enrolled and nothing else.
conclusions.so_what: 97 are at Monty Tech, which Lunenburg helps fund; 38 at charters or virtual schools.

conclusions.basis: dls-override-votes.csv, override rows only, counted per town over every year the file covers.
conclusions.claim: Ashby has put 60 override questions and won 7. Lunenburg put 10, won 4.
conclusions.detail: Across the six towns that share a border with Lunenburg, the number of Proposition 2½ questions put since FY1990 runs from 0 to 60. Ashby is the highest at 60 questions and 7 wins; Leominster has never put one. Lunenburg sits at 10 and 4. The towns are adjacent, their school costs move with the same contracts and the same state aid formula, and their appetite for asking differs by a factor of 6.

loud_put.unit: override questions Ashby has put to its voters since FY1990, of which 7 carried

conclusions.not_shown: What a question was FOR. The file gives a department and a description, and a town that asks nine times for a fire truck is not a town that asks nine times for teachers. Nor does a low count mean a town never needed the money: it may have cut instead, used a debt exclusion — which is outside the levy limit and not in this file at all — or never brought a question that would have lost.
conclusions.so_what: Adjacent towns under the same cost pressure differ 6x in how often they ask.

destinations.district: TEC Connections Academy Commonwealth Virtual School District
Sizer School: A North Central Charter Essential (District)

grain: Two calendars, never mixed. Tax figures are FY2026, the last year the Division of Local Services has a rate for every town: an AVERAGE single-family bill on an AVERAGE single-family assessment, which is not any one house. School figures are SY2025, the last year DESE has published spending: dollars per full-time-equivalent pupil, ALL FUNDS, so state aid and grants are inside it and it is not what the town raises. An override row is a question PUT to a ballot, not a dollar levied.
not_established: Whose comparison set is right. The six neighbours are computed from boundary polygons and are a fact; the five peers are OUR choice, and nothing in the town’s own record names a cohort of comparable communities for tax purposes. The twins are a distance in a space we chose the axes of.
What any destination costs. A count of children enrolled somewhere is not a tuition, an assessment or a share of one, and nothing here says which fund pays for any of it.

The tax burden behind a regional district. Nashoba, North Middlesex, Ayer Shirley and Montachusett are funded by assessments on member towns with different bills, and no dataset here holds the membership lists or the apportionment, so no single bill can stand for any of them.
Whether a town spending more per pupil educates a child better. Per-pupil spending is an input. Nothing in this report is an outcome measure.
Which way any correlation runs. Every figure here is a cross-section of one year across many towns, which cannot separate a town choosing a higher bill from a town able to afford one.
